text.p: Finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Tuesday painted a rosy picture of Britain's economic prospects as he unveiled a pre-election budget overshadowed by embarrassing leaks of his tax and spending plans.

Clarke, whose budget is crucial to the ruling Conservatives' hopes of winning a fifth consecutive term in office, said he intended to make "responsible progress" on the party's tax-cutting agenda while getting borrowing down faster.
"This is not a reckless budget on tax and spending. In the run-up to Christmas I am not going to play Santa Claus, but this year I do not have to play Scrooge either," he said.
Clarke said he expected growth in the British economy to accelerate to 3.5 percent in 1997, from 2.5 percent this year, fuelled by a rise of more than four percent in consumer spending.

Despite the buoyant outlook, which he said would keep Britain the fastest-growing major economy in Europe next year, Clarke said he expected to reach his target for underlying inflation of 2.5 percent.
Although inflation picked up to 3.3 percent last month, he said the risk to the recovery from rising prices was a good way off because commodity prices and wages were under control.

"The British economy is in its fifth successive year of steady, healthy economic growth, with falling unemployment and low inflation. These are the best circumstances we have faced for a generation. This is a Rolls Royce recovery -- built to last," the chancellor of the exchequer said.
As Clarke spoke, a high-level investigation was under way into the leak of a sheaf of documents to the Daily Mirror newspaper with details of key parts of the budget.

The leak, the worst in half a century, acutely embarrassed Prime Minister John Major's government, which is struggling to shake off the perception that it is losing its once-sure touch after 17-1/2 years in power.
The Daily Mirror held back from publishing the documents, which Major's office confirmed were genuine.
But other papers said Clarke would round off his budget by cutting the basic income tax rate to 23 percent from 24 percent.

London stocks, following a soaring New York market, hit new highs ahead of the budget as the leaks reinforced expectations of a prudent package of measures crafted to appeal to voters without causing an already robust economy to overheat.
The Labour party, in opposition since 1979, revelled in the government's misfortunes over the leak.

"How can anyone trust Kenneth Clarke to run the economy when he loses half his budget? This is just another reflection of the shambles which at present passes for government," the party's campaigns chief, Brian Wilson, said.
Budget details are among the government's most closely guarded secrets. Labour finance minister Hugh Dalton had to resign in 1947 after leaking tax details to a journalist.

The leak posed another severe test for Clarke, who was forced to make a statement to parliament on Monday to reassure anti-European Conservatives that the government was not trying to sneak through rules governing the European Union's planned single currency.
